title: Poles, zeros and Bode plots of circuits

sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
Each energy-storage element in a circuit usually contributes a pole, and the time constants of the circuit set the corner frequencies. A pole at \(1/(R C)\) comes from a capacitor with the resistance it sees. A zero appears when some path makes the output vanish at a particular frequency, for example a capacitor bypassing a resistor.

To get a Bode plot of a circuit, write \(H(s)\) with impedances, factor it into standard first-order terms, and read off the corners. When two poles are far apart, each can be estimated from the resistance seen by its own capacitor with the other capacitor treated as open or short. That is the open-circuit time-constant idea.

Amplifier stages are a common case: a gain stage with a load capacitor gives a low-pass corner at the output node, and a coupling capacitor gives a high-pass corner at low frequency. The band between them is the **midband**.
sections.figure_alt: Band-pass Bode magnitude: rising at low frequency, flat midband, falling at high frequency.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: A stage has midband gain 25, a 4.7 µF coupling capacitor into 10 kΩ and a 12 pF load on a 39 kΩ output. Then \(f_L = 3.4\ \mathrm{Hz}\) and \(f_H = 340\ \mathrm{kHz}\). The Bode magnitude is flat at 28 dB between them, rising at \(+20\) below and falling at \(-20\) above.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Using the wrong resistance for a capacitor's time constant.
- Merging two widely separated corners.
- Forgetting that a coupling capacitor causes a low-frequency corner.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: The same corner-reading is needed to find amplifier loop gain and compensation.
